In [[mathematics]], the '''Hall–Littlewood polynomials''' are [[Ring of symmetric functions|symmetric functions]] depending on a parameter ''t'' and a [[partition (number theory)|partition]] &lambda;.  They are [[Schur polynomial|Schur functions]] when ''t'' is 0 and monomial symmetric functions when ''t'' is 1 and are special cases of [[Macdonald polynomials]].
They were first defined indirectly by  [[Philip Hall]] using the [[Hall algebra]], and later defined directly by [[Dudley E. Littlewood]] (1961).

==Definition==
The Hall–Littlewood polynomial ''P'' is defined by
:<math>P_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n;t) = \left( \prod_{i\geq 0} \prod_{j=1}^{m(i)} \frac{1-t}{1-t^{j}} \right)
{\sum_{w\in S_n}w\left(x_1^{\lambda_1}\cdots x_n^{\lambda_n}\prod_{i<j}\frac{x_i-tx_j}{x_i-x_j}\right)},
</math>
where &lambda; is a partition of at most ''n'' with elements &lambda;<sub>''i''</sub>, and ''m''(''i'') elements equal to ''i'',  and ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> is the [[symmetric group]] of order ''n''!.


As an example,
:<math> P_{42}(x_1,x_2;t) = x_1^4 x_2^2 + x_1^2 x_2^4 + (1-t) x_1^3 x_2^3 </math>

===Specializations===

We have that <math>P_\lambda(x;1) = m_\lambda(x)</math>,  <math>P_\lambda(x;0) = s_\lambda(x)</math> and 
<math>P_\lambda(x;-1) = P_\lambda(x)</math> where the latter is the Schur ''P'' polynomials.

==Properties==

Expanding the [[Schur polynomials]] in terms of the Hall–Littlewood polynomials, one has
:<math> s_\lambda(x) = \sum_\mu K_{\lambda\mu}(t) P_\mu(x,t)</math>
where <math>K_{\lambda\mu}(t)</math> are the [[Kostka polynomial|Kostka–Foulkes polynomials]].
Note that as <math>t=1</math>, these reduce to the ordinary Kostka coefficients.

A combinatorial description for the Kostka–Foulkes polynomials was given by Lascoux and Schützenberger,
:<math>K_{\lambda\mu}(t) = \sum_{T \in SSYT(\lambda,\mu)} t^{\mathrm{charge}(T)}</math>
where "charge" is a certain combinatorial statistic on semistandard Young tableaux,
and the sum is taken over the set <math> SSYT(\lambda,\mu)</math> of all semi-standard Young tableaux ''T'' with shape ''λ'' and type&nbsp;''μ''.
